name: GSK-971086
lead: GSK-971086 (also written GSK971086) is an investigational non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) from the indole chemical class, developed by GlaxoSmithKline and investigated for sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) and androgen deficiency.[1][2] SARMs are designed to activate the androgen receptor in muscle and bone while sparing reproductive tissues such as the prostate, which is why the class is discussed in physique circles as a route to more muscle and lean mass.[1]

A Phase I trial registered in 2007 tested safety, tolerability and blood levels in healthy adult males after a single dose and after seven days of dosing.[2] Wikipedia lists the compound as having been discontinued after Phase I.[1] No results for appearance or muscle-building have been published for this specific compound.

The better-known GSK compound in the class is GSK-2881078, an indole SARM that reached Phase II for cachexia and COPD-related muscle weakness.[1] GSK-971086 itself is not an item that appears to have reached the consumer gray market in the way other SARMs have.

chain: Selective activation of the androgen receptor in muscle and bone
Intended gain in lean mass and strength
angle.text: As a SARM, GSK-971086 was developed to increase muscle mass in conditions like sarcopenia. Any appearance benefit would come from the potential for more lean mass; the compound was not developed past a safety trial in healthy men.

paras: Wikipedia lists GSK971086 as an indole-class SARM investigated for sarcopenia that did not progress beyond Phase I.[1] The registered trial (NCT00540553) began in August 2007, enrolled 126 participants, and is listed as completed; it examined safety, tolerability and blood levels after one dose and after seven days of dosing in healthy adult males.[2]

Other GSK compounds in the class include GSK-2881078, an indole SARM taken to Phase II for cachexia and linked to a COPD muscle-weakness trial, and GSK-2849466, which was discontinued after Phase I.[1]

SARMs are described as activating the androgen receptor selectively, aiming to build muscle and bone while sparing the prostate. Proposed explanations include that they are not converted by 5-alpha-reductase and that tissue-specific coregulator expression changes their effects, although the mechanism is still debated.[1] In a Phase III trial, enobosarm increased lean body mass without a significant functional improvement, and the FDA did not approve it partly because evidence of better physical performance was lacking.[1]

No SARM had been approved by the FDA or EMA as of 2023, and WADA has banned the class since 2008.[1] Reported adverse effects of SARMs in trials have been described as mild and infrequent, with raised liver enzymes and lowered HDL cholesterol noted, while case reports link recreational use to drug-induced liver injury.[1] Gray-market SARM sellers have faced criminal convictions and fines.[1]

One Phase I trial (NCT00540553, n=126, healthy adult males, started 2007) examined safety, tolerability and blood levels after one dose and after seven days of dosing; it is listed as completed.[2] Results have not been published in a form found, and no efficacy trial has been reported.

timeline.event: Phase I safety and pharmacokinetic trial begins in healthy males.[2]

card.summary: A discontinued GSK indole-class SARM that never got past Phase I; no efficacy data exist.
card.note: Investigational only; not approved and no published efficacy results.

quick.overview:
GSK-971086 is an experimental SARM from GlaxoSmithKline that was studied for sarcopenia and androgen deficiency.

It was tested in a single Phase I safety trial in healthy men and then discontinued. It is not a marketed drug.
quick.mechanism: SARMs aim to switch on androgen receptors selectively, favoring muscle and bone over reproductive tissues. This compound belongs to the indole chemical class.
quick.risks: No results from its Phase I trial are public in the sources reviewed. The SARM class is unapproved, banned in sport by WADA, and linked in case reports to liver injury with recreational use.
